facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 a public demonstration entitled the 'March of Millions' was held in central Moscow.
The 'March of Millions' demonstration on 6 May 2012 was held to protest against the allegedly rigged presidential elections.
According to the applicant, on 6 May 2012 he arrived at Kaluzhskaya Square to take part in the 'March of Millions' demonstration.
According to the applicant, on 6 May 2012 he walked with other participants from Kaluzhskaya Square to Bolotnaya Square.
According to the applicant, when passage to the stage of the rally taking place along the embankment was opened, the applicant went in that direction.
The applicant pleaded not guilty at trial and testified that he had decided to attend the public gathering on 6 May 2012.
The applicant was arrested by the police on 6 May 2012 and taken to a police station before being released shortly after.
On 26 July 2012 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having participated in acts of mass disorder on 6 May 2012.
On 1 August 2012 charges were brought against the applicant under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation (participation in acts of mass disorder accompanied by violence).
On 21 February 2014 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow found the applicant guilty as charged.
The applicant was sentenced to three years and six months' imprisonment.

Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the organisation of mass disorder, accompanied by violence, riot, arson, destruction of property, the use of firearms, explosives and explosive devices, as well as armed resistance to a public official, shall be punishable by four to ten years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that participation in the types of mass disorder provided for by Article 212 § 1 shall be punishable by three to eight years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the use of violence which does not endanger life or health, or the threat to use such violence against a public official or his relatives in connection with the performance of his or her duties, shall be punishable by a fine of up to 200,000 roubles or an equivalent of the convicted person's wages for 18 months, or community service for up to five years, or up to five years' deprivation of liberty.

A summary of the relevant domestic law provisions governing pre-trial detention and the practice of the domestic courts in such matters is set out in Zherebin v. Russia (no. 51445/09, §§ 16-25, 24 March 2016).

The ten defendants in the criminal case before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow were charged with participation in acts of mass disorder and committing acts of violence against police officers.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that unidentified persons called those present at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012 to use violence, which led to mass disorder accompanied by the use of violence against public officials in connection with the performance of their duties and the destruction of property.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant used violence against Police Officer T. which did not endanger his life or health.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that from 5 p.m. to 9.40 p.m. on 6 May 2012, when unidentified participants of acts of mass disorder tried to break the police cordon, the applicant acting intentionally grabbed Police Officer T.'s hand and pulled it off the person whom T. was arresting, thus impeding his apprehension, which caused T. pain.
According to the applicant, the police started to disperse the protesters at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012, using excessive force and beating them with truncheons.
According to the applicant, in response to the police dispersal, the protesters dragged metal barriers into place to protect themselves from the police.
According to the applicant, at one point he observed a protester in a green T-shirt who five or six police officers were holding and beating with truncheons.
According to the applicant, he grabbed the protester in the green T-shirt and pulled him back, trying to protect him from the truncheon blows.
Police Officer T. testified that the applicant had caused him pain but had not inflicted any injuries.
During the hearing on 5 September 2013 the applicant and his lawyers applied to deprive Police Officer T. of victim status because no harm had been caused to him.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant, who was wearing a surgical mask to hide his face, together with unidentified persons, tried to liberate those arrested by the police for a breach of public order and pushed the police officers away.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant used violence against Police Officer T. which did not endanger his life or health.

The applicant testified that at the stage area he saw the mass beating of people by police officers and participants of the rally starting to bring forward metal barriers and to put them close to the police officers, trying to protect themselves from the latter.
The applicant testified that he saw a group of five or six police officers who were trying to seize a young man in a green T-shirt and were hitting the man with their truncheons.

The applicant testified that, considering the young man in the green T-shirt was in danger because the police actions were unlawful, he tried to snatch him from the officers' hands by grasping the young man's waistband, pulling it and turning his back to protect him from the truncheon blows.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow considered the defendants' arguments that they were protecting somebody from police officers or happened to be victims of the police's use of force as farfetched and aimed at the mitigation of their responsibility.
